palette.notes: No frames or metrics here. Loom's DOS release was 16-colour EGA (wiki); his cycled scenes run on 8-bit indexed palettes where a few slots are reserved to rotate. Deep blue/violet shadows, warm light sources.

lighting: Time of day and weather are carried by the palette: the same drawing reads as dawn, dusk or night because the indexed colours change, not the pixels. Light comes from a sky or a lit window.
silhouette: Landscapes first: layered trees, cliffs, ruins and water read as big dark shapes against a bright sky band; figures, when present, are tiny.

motion.timing: Nothing measured. Motion is palette rotation: water, rain, snow and fire 'move' by cycling a strip of colour slots, so the loop runs forever with zero redrawn frames.

texture: Heavy hand-placed dithering to fake gradients in skies and water; dithering also builds the bands that colour cycling travels through.
camera: Locked wide establishing shot; the canvas-cycle viewer only zooms. Stillness of the frame makes the cycled areas the only thing moving.
sound: The Canvas Cycle viewer offers optional ambient sound per scene.

acting.enters: No characters act; the scene is the performer.
acting.acts: Waterfalls, rain and reflections shimmer in place while the rest stays frozen.
acting.depth: Depth from atmospheric value steps: far layers lighter and bluer, near layers darker.

techniques: colour cycling: rotate a reserved strip of palette slots to animate water, rain, snow
palette swap for time of day on one drawing
dithered gradient bands that double as cycle paths
atmospheric perspective: lighter, bluer far layers
frozen frame + one moving element (cinemagraph logic)
feel: frozen wide landscape + one strip of cycled colour (water, rain) = alive and calm without redrawing
for_fred: Use a cycled-colour ambient loop (pond ripples, sign glow) behind Fred so the scene stays alive while he is off screen; then his re-entry is the only new motion and reads instantly. A palette shift (day to dusk) can mark a time jump between his appearances.
